topic: Topic 2: Real Numbers, Supremum/Infimum & Density Theorem
question: State and prove the Density Theorem for rational numbers in $\mathbb{R}$.
concept_tested: Density Theorem for Rational Numbers and Irrationals in $\mathbb{R}$ (Complete Essay)
approach: State the theorem, use the Archimedean Property to establish existence of denominator $n$, apply the well-ordering principle / integer bounds for numerator $m$, handle all sign cases, and prove the corollary on density of irrational numbers.

solution_steps.title: Statement of the Density Theorem
solution_steps.math: \forall x, y \in \mathbb{R} \text{ with } x < y, \; \exists q \in \mathbb{Q} \text{ such that } x < q < y
solution_steps.explanation: Every non-empty open interval $(x, y) \subset \mathbb{R}$ contains at least one (and hence infinitely many) rational numbers.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: $x > 0$ — Choosing the Denominator $n$
solution_steps.math: y - x > 0 \implies \exists n \in \mathbb{N} \text{ such that } n > \frac{1}{y - x} \iff ny - nx > 1
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property of $\mathbb{R}$, since $y - x > 0$, there exists a natural number $n$ whose reciprocal is less than $y-x$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: Choosing the Numerator $m$
solution_steps.math: S = \{k \in \mathbb{N} : k > nx\} \ne \emptyset \implies m = \min S \implies m - 1 \le nx < m
solution_steps.explanation: By the Archimedean Property, $S$ is non-empty. By the Well-Ordering Principle of $\mathbb{N}$, $S$ has a least element $m$. Then $m-1 \notin S$, meaning $m-1 \le nx$, and $m \in S$, meaning $nx < m$.

solution_steps.title: Case 1: Enclosing $m$ in $(nx, ny)$
solution_steps.math: m \le nx + 1 < ny \implies nx < m < ny \implies x < \frac{m}{n} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Since $ny - nx > 1$, we have $nx + 1 < ny$. Dividing through by $n > 0$ yields the rational number $q = m/n$ satisfying $x < q < y$.

solution_steps.title: Case 2: General Case ($x \le 0$)
solution_steps.math: \text{If } x \le 0, \text{ by Archimedean Property } \exists k \in \mathbb{N} \text{ s.t. } k > |x| \implies x + k > 0
solution_steps.explanation: Now $0 < x + k < y + k$. By Case 1, there exists $q' \in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $x + k < q' < y + k$. Subtracting integer $k$ gives $q = q' - k \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $x < q < y$.

solution_steps.title: Corollary: Density of Irrational Numbers
solution_steps.math: \exists r \in \mathbb{Q} \setminus \{0\} \text{ s.t. } \frac{x}{\sqrt{2}} < r < \frac{y}{\sqrt{2}} \implies x < r\sqrt{2} < y
solution_steps.explanation: Since $r$ is a non-zero rational and $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, the product $z = r\sqrt{2}$ is irrational, proving that irrationals are also dense in $\mathbb{R}$.

final_answer: Every open interval $(x, y)$ contains a rational number $q = m/n$ and an irrational number $z = r\sqrt{2}$. Thus both $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$ are dense in $\mathbb{R}$.
exam_tip: In a 10-mark essay, always state the Archimedean property explicitly, detail both the positive and negative cases, and include the irrational density corollary.
